## Claude_Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

3	# Climb batch 6.5
4	
5	## 1. For Pavol
6	
7	Batch 6.5 is the repair batch of the plan's phase 2b: what the conformance reviews of batches 3 to 6 found, with three findings of the reviews of batches 6b, 7 and 7R, repaired before phase 3 (`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`, phase 2b). A rung is one fix, built test-first by one worker in its own copy of the tree and judged by a second worker, the skeptic, before the batch is merged and the whole test suite (the gate) runs once.
8	
9	In plain words: the batch fixes six defects of the compiled path that the switch-over and microGPT's parallel run would meet (a class-loading race at four threads, a parallel task and a generic method that fail to load, two dispatch defects, and a `typecase` whose bound name the code generator never binds, which is why the compiled `cast` never matched); makes both paths refuse a size beyond `NN32` as you decided; makes walk's last integer natives, `LCM` on the unsigned types, `^` and `CHOOSE`, raise `IntegerOverflow` where the result does not fit, instead of a wrong number or an error no `catch` sees; repairs the range bodies that relied on wrapping, with the reorder you chose for the strided distance; makes `RR32` a sibling of `RR64` as the specification and the team's own compiler library have it; and brings the specification and our test messages up to date with what earlier batches built. It runs as two runs of one record, G and P first and then E and V from the tree they land: G first as you decided, and P and V apart because they edit the same two specification files, while a run of all four would be the longest yet; one word runs the four as one (below).
10	
11	**No question is open.** The draft's one question, when walk switches a numeral to `IntLiteral`, which the probe showed cannot happen before answer 8's promotion rule on either path (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-6.5/NOTES.md`, section 1), you answered on 2026-09-27: batch N builds the inference rule, whose number case is the promotion rule, together with the numeral switch, on both paths, and that closes this question (POSITIONS 2026-09-27, the numerics plans, decision 3; `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`, phase 3, item 4). So this batch writes row 443's owed test, rung G makes answer 7's identities independent of a numeral's type, and rows 79, 432, 437 and 443 stay open for batch N.
12	
13	**The rungs.**
14	- **G, generics at run time on the compiled path.** The class loader's first-load race at four threads (row 417), a parallel task in a generic declaration (row 419), a generic method building over two sets of parameters (row 420), the two dispatch defects with the measured 43-line fix, and a `typecase` or `catch` clause's bound name (row 351, which is the cause of row 426, at `cast` and at the library's second such clause, `andCondCombine`); answer 7's identity functions made to pass values of the right type through `cast`.
15	- **P, the text.** The specification gains the integer rules you decided on 2026-09-22 (the shifts, `narrow`, the overflow of an unrepresentable shift) and a corrected coercion example (row 394); the rational type's listing states the algebra the library declares; the test messages whose specification line numbers earlier batches moved are re-anchored; the scalar block's comment stops naming a shape answer 9 refuses; and the owed expected-failure tests of rows 440 and 443 are written.
16	- **E, a value beyond its type's range.** Both paths refuse a size beyond `NN32` (`ZZ32` for an `int` size), and walk reads the sizes in range exactly, where today it truncates them to 32 bits (row 418); `NN32`'s `LCM` raises `IntegerOverflow` where the result does not fit, instead of a wrong number, and so do the nine natives rung O left, `^` and `CHOOSE` on the four fixed widths and `NN64`'s `LCM` (row 347 closes with them); and the three range bodies that answered right at the integer bounds only by wrapping, with the sequential ranges that step past their last element, are reordered on the checked operators, as you decided for the strided distance (rows 450, 451).
17	- **V, `RR32` a sibling.** `RR32` stops being a subtype of `RR64`; `RR64` converts from it; its arithmetic takes an `RR32` (row 435); one sentence in the number chapter names it.
18	
19	**Read from the record, not asked.** Each follows from a decision on record or from a probe; one word from you changes it.
20	- **Two runs.** The first run, batch 6.5, is G and P; the second, batch 6.5b, is E and V, cut from the tree the first lands. G goes first by your decision: its rows (417, 419, 420, 351, 426) are on microGPT's compiled run (POSITIONS 2026-09-27, the numerics plans, decision 5; `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`, phase 2b), and batch N may take the slot after this run. The rule that a batch carries one rung touching Java or Scala (`explorations/coordinator/batched-climb-plan.md` section 5, rule 3) does not force the split: its reason is the cost of a full rebuild in each copy, and batches 3.5, 4 and 5 ran two such rungs, as batch 7's second run, batch 7b, will (C and W). Two things do. P and V both edit `Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, and both add their Appendix I entries at one place of `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, after its last revision entry, since batch 7C rung X's "The traits that extend a closed trait" (`:1246` at cd9305c2d), before "Passages not yet revised" (`:1340`), which in one run is a same-point hunk the gather resolves by hand (section 4). And a run of the four is 8 to 11 hours in one piece, with G the largest rung, under a container that has died before (`explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md`), with a held push holding four rungs instead of two. So each run pairs the rung in Java or Scala with one that is not, G with P and E with V, and neither pair shares a declaration (section 4). The price of the split is one more gather and gate, about 8 agents, 2M tokens and 2 hours. One word runs the four as one batch (section 7's `RUN`), with section 4's order for the two shared files.
21	- **Rows 450 and 451 go to E.** Their repair is decided: the distance reordered so that no step leaves the range, the checked operators kept, and emptiness tested before the distance, as you decided for the strided distance (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, rung O of climb batch 4; the rows' notes). Rung O's batch and batch 7R each left them out of their rungs, and at the switch-over the compiled path runs these bodies (`explorations/reviews/batch-6b-7-conformance.md` finding 2, `explorations/reviews/batch-7R-conformance.md` finding 5). E or P could carry them under the batch rules: in either run the bodies share no declaration with the other rung's edits, and they are Fortress, so each run keeps one rung in Java or Scala. E carries them because a change to every sequential range's step needs the interpreter corpus compared before and after, which E runs anyway for its natives, so one comparison measures both; P stays a text rung whose checker count cannot move. In the second run E and V then share `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` on declarations far apart (section 4).

The specification settles them (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-155`), and walk raises its catchable `IntegerOverflow` for them by the rule of your decisions on row 379 and on the unsigned types (POSITIONS 2026-09-24, ledger row 379; 2026-09-26, the fifth batch-5 answer), which rung O built for the arithmetic natives. They share `NN32.java` and one test with `NN32`'s `LCM`, which E already carries. They get one new row, which closes with them, and row 347 closes if `Int$Pow` and `Int$Choose` are its last uncatchable callers, as the review reads.
23	- **Row 426 fits this batch.** Its cause, traced by the probe, is two things: the code generator never binds a `typecase` clause's name (row 351, whose fix is recorded in the row), and `cast[\ZZ32\](0)` passes a numeral, which is correctly not a `ZZ32` on the compiled path (`NOTES.md`, section 2). Both are small, so G carries them. What waits for the switch-over is only the end-to-end check of a compiled `SUM`'s identity, because the compiler's own library has no generic `SUM`.
24	- **`RR32` a sibling needs no question.** The specification says the number types are mutually exclusive (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:536`), the later Types chapter keeps that (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick:977-978`), Chase cut the subtype in 2009 ("RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64", `6896886fb`), Steele's retrospective draws the two floats as siblings, the compiler library has `RR64` converting from `RR32`, the specification's own worked example converts an `RR32` into `RR64` arithmetic, and your answer 8's rule makes an exact conversion a coercion. The probe found nothing that relies on the subtype beyond `RR32`'s own declarations and three library sites, which the rung restates (`NOTES.md`, section 6); with `RR32`'s operators declared in its api as `RR64`'s are, the corpus changes no verdict but that of row 435's expected failure, which passes, and no team test line.
25	- **A size read as a value keeps the checker's type.** Your decision's words, a `nat` parameter "is an `NN32` value", admit two readings, the range alone or the type as well. The record takes the range: a size beyond `NN32` is refused, and the compiled checker keeps typing a size read as a value as `IntLiteral`, which converts into `NN32` wherever the specification's sentence names. Typing it `NN32` itself would refuse, at the switch-over, the one library's own bodies that read a size into `ZZ32` index arithmetic (`for i <- seq(1#(s0-1))` at `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2426` and `:2807`, `b0#s0` at `:2462` and `:2470`, `self[0#n]` at `:4102`), where an `NN32` beside a `ZZ32` needs batch N's inference rule, and about 16 compiled test files that read a size into `ZZ32` or `ZZ64`, a conversion the compiler library lacks. It comes back with batch N's numeral switch and the array design; `PLAN.md`'s item 25, whether a `nat` parameter may be a range's component, is the same question asked from the range's side, which the review of batch 7R asks to settle before batch N (its finding 1).
26	- **The rational type's listing states the library's algebra.** The number chapters describe the one library (your answer 6 and the rule that the gather checks the chapters against the library), and the library's `QQ` carries the group, ring and order traits `SUM` and `PROD` need. The chapter's listing gives `QQ` only `Number`, because 0/0 breaks the laws; P states the library's traits with one sentence that their laws hold away from 0/0 and the infinities, as `RR64`'s hold away from NaN. Your parked question on whether `QQ` holds 0/0 at all is untouched.
27	- **The integer rules go into the specification's prose, in the team's layered form (S1),** as every change to the specification since rung S (POSITIONS 2026-09-24, the requirement on the plan).
28	- **The stops are reversible.** Each stop this record reserves for you lands and is listed for your review; none holds a push or the next run (POSITIONS 2026-09-27, the stops; the protocol's first hard rule).
29	- **Row 417's gated home is a program in the gate's four-thread stage,** as phase 2b says. The stage is in the script, outside the manifest, so the coordinator makes that change with the first run's splice, since G runs first (section 8).
30	- **The dispatch fix covers template dispatchers, as measured.** The probe re-ran it on today's tree: the three legal programs that die today print the specification's answers. Generic dotted methods and a dispatcher that is not a template keep the defect; G records them.
31	
32	**What the batch leaves out.**
33	- The numeral switch, batch N's (section 1), and with it rows 79, 432 and 437 and PLAN's item 19.
34	- From the reviews, what the plan already holds elsewhere: the checked narrowing after the switch-over and the `asString` overflow (phase 4); the product-of-sizes storage (item 15); rung C's two points (item 16); the where-clause sentence (item 14); rows 446 and 447 (items 17 and 18); a judge striking a candidate (asked 2026-09-27).
35	- The tuple shifts of `Library/RangeInternals.fss` that subtract a whole tuple (batch 3.5 and 4's review, smaller findings): no row and no probe yet.
36	- Row 453, the compiler prelude's range midpoint and its `#` at the integer bounds: the prelude leaves at the switch-over, and E's repair of the one library's bodies is what the compiled path then runs.
37	- Record repairs the reviews name (the stale `FACTS.md` line on the exclusion fork, row 97's note, row 360's options): the coordinator's record work, not a rung.
38	- Row 424's repair, row 433's fusion pairs and row 441: phase 3 or later, as the plan has them.
39	
40	**Cost.** By arithmetic, not measured, from the batch records: a rung costs 3 to 5 agents, 1.0M to 2.0M tokens and 1.2 to 2.0 hours of the two-agent queue, and a run's tail from the gather to the commit about 8 agents, 2M tokens and 2 hours (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-7.md` section 1, "Cost"). The first run, G and P: 16 to 20 agents, 5M to 8M tokens, 5 to 8 hours, G being the largest rung. The second, E and V: 14 to 18 agents, 5M to 8M tokens, 5 to 8 hours, each rung with three passes over the interpreter corpus (30 to 34 minutes a pass on this box, `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-6.5/probes/rr32/passes-machine.txt`), which load the box together where they overlap. As one run of four: 20 to 28 agents, 7M to 11M tokens, 8 to 11 hours, one tail fewer. The probes cost about 1M tokens. Two agents run at a time; the box has 4 CPUs, 16 GB and 11 GB of free disk at the review (`df -h /`, the probes' worktrees removed, batch 6b's still present).
41	
42	**What "go" commits you to.** Two gos, one per run. The first: the compiled path's class loader takes a lock on first load, and parallel tasks, generic methods, dispatch and `typecase` bindings work where they failed; answer 7's identity functions are respelled with the same values; the gate's four-thread stage gains G's program; the specification states the integer rules of 2026-09-22 and a corrected example, in the S1 form; the rational type's listing states the library's traits; a handful of our test messages get new line numbers; the scalar block's comment is reworded; two expected-failure tests are added. 191	
192	**The answers this rung follows.** Section 1's one question is answered, and it changes nothing in this rung.
193	
194	**The problem.** `RR32` is the one number type of the one library still below another: `value object RR32 extends RR64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:47`, `.fss:203`), and `RR64` comprises `{ Float, FloatLiteral, RR32 }` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:291-294`). An `RR32` value is then also an `RR64` value, which the specification forbids: "These types are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them" (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:536`), kept by the later Types chapter (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick:977-978`). `RR32`'s binary natives declare `b:RR64` and read it with `getRR32()`, so an `RR32` with any other number ends the run with an `InterpreterBug` (row 435; `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXRR32MixedRungF.fss`). By reading, an `RR64`-typed value may be an `RR32` at run time, whose operators answer `RR32`, which unboxing by static type in phase 6 could not follow (`explorations/reviews/batch-6-conformance.md`, finding 3). It entered batch 6 as its record's reading, not a decision.

196	**The decisions.** Route A (POSITIONS 2026-09-24): the number types siblings under `Number`, each carrying its own algebra. Answer 8 (2026-09-26): an exact conversion is a coercion, a lossy one explicit; every `RR32` value is exact in `RR64`. The number chapters describe the library (answer 6; 2026-09-26, the number chapters under S2), so the chapter names `RR32` once it is a sibling, in the S1 form.

The compiler library's `RR32` is a sibling that `RR64` converts from (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:433-435`, `:475-476`). The specification's worked example computes an `RR32` with an `RR64` by `RR64`'s declaration after a coercion (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:861-898`). Chase's `6896886fb` (2009-08-31) cut the subtype in the compiler library, "RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64", and Steele's retrospective draws the floats as siblings (`research/extracts/SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md:159-161`). The flat library's `RR64` is the model of what a float carries at its own type (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:291-294` and its body). The probe built two shapes (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-6.5/probes/rr32/`; `NOTES.md` section 6). - The testSystem shards move by the two new tests, compared by their sum.

## 9. The defects, and their homes

- **Row 440** (walk's `0/0 = 0/0` and `0/0 CMP 0/0`): home 2, `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXRationalUnorderedRungP.fss`, asserting `numbers.tex:365-369` and `:375-379`. The fix, `QQ`'s `=`, is not this rung's; the library's comment chooses the answer on purpose (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:568`).
- **Row 443** (walk's refusal of `s: RR64 = 3000000000`): home 2, `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXNumeralFloatRungP.fss`, asserting `conversions-coercions.tex:117-118`, `:158-159` and `numbers.tex:43`. The fix is batch N's numeral switch.
- **Row 394**: repaired in the specification's text, the example as revised run on both paths by the probes of section 2. No gated test, since no test can go red for a prose edit; `ProjectFortress/tests/CoercionMostSpecificRungC.fss` already gates the shape with its own names.
- **Two garbled properties with `shift`** (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:789`, `:810`, the `%%` sources, and their typeset lines): found while making the list, by reading. No decision covers them, and the library declares none of their methods, so the repair is not chosen here. Home 3 by the prefix's terms, the specification being the defective text and nothing settling the intended one: a ledger row (record.md; provisionally 493, row 500 at the gather, which also carries its skeptic's R1). Their probe is the list's entry L5; no program can run them.
- **The compiled prelude's integer gaps**: `NN32` and `NN64` have no `LSHIFT`, `RSHIFT`, `GCD` or `LCM`, and `ZZ` has no `narrow`. They are closed by the switch-over. They become a note to row 442, which records the prelude's gaps against the revised number chapters; each is measured by reading `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss` (the trait boundaries at `:517-576`, `:754-817`, `:819-881`). Since the judge's repair of climb batch 6.5 each is measured and gated as an expected failure, promoted at the switch-over, as `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is: `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNNShiftRungP`, `XXXNNGcdLcmRungP` and `XXXZZNarrowRungP` (rows 442 and 349; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-6.5/judge-repair/prelude-integer-xxx.txt`).

## 10. The stops

- **"Normative text for a rule neither path runs"**, met on part of the work. The overview's new sentence (`Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:264-268`) says that a `GCD` or `LCM` a fixed-size type cannot hold throws `IntegerOverflow`, "by the rule for integer results above" (the gather's wording for the rung's "as for its other operators"). For `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` both paths run it. For `NN32` and `NN64`, walk's `LCM` answers a wrong number or wraps (`NN32.java:149-155`, `UnsignedLong.java:150-156`; climb batch 6.5b's rung E repairs them), and the compiled prelude declares neither operator. The sentence applies the specification's existing general rule (`opr-overview.tex:154-155`), which Pavol's decision on the unsigned types extends to them (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, the fifth batch-5 answer), so it is not a new rule; it is listed here because no path runs it on the unsigned types today. The stop is reversible, and it is lifted by POSITIONS 2026-09-27, on the stops a batch record reserves.
- None else. Nothing under `Specification-1.0-frozen/` changed (`git diff --stat b797d8037 -- Specification-1.0-frozen` is empty). content.content:
An integer type coerces from each other integer type all of whose values it holds,
as listed above; every other conversion between integer types is written explicitly.

Among the explicit conversions, the method \VAR{narrow} converts a value of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and a value of
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} to \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, by keeping its low 32 bits: the result
is the value of the narrower type that is congruent to the argument modulo
\EXP{2^{32}}.
A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other wraps, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.

The operators \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT} shift the bits of an integer of any of
the five types by a count of any integer type, and return a value of the type of
the integer shifted.
On \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,k)} and
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,-k)}.
On a fixed-size type of width \VAR{n}, for a nonnegative count \VAR{k},
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\lfloor x/2^{k} \rfloor}, and
\EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is the value of the type that is congruent to
\EXP{x \cdot 2^{k}} modulo \EXP{2^{n}}: the bits shifted out are lost, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.
So a count at or beyond the width gives \EXP{0} for a left shift, and for a right
shift \EXP{0}, or \EXP{-1} if \VAR{x} is negative.
A negative count shifts the other way: \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} (-k)} is
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k}, and \EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} (-k)} is \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k}.
The count is read by its value, whatever its type: an \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} count of
\EXP{2^{63}} or more is beyond the width, not negative.
\revision{revival-shifts}{The Working Draft of February 2011 named neither
\VAR{narrow} nor \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT}, which \library\ declare on the
integer types; the two paragraphs above state the rules the revival decided for
them.}

------
on the two's-complement representation of the integer;
positive values of \VAR{k} shifts the bits to the left,
and negative values of \VAR{k} shifts the bits to the right.
The result is exact for a count of any size, and a result too large for the
implementation to represent throws an \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
On \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, the operators \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT} compute this
shift with the count and with its negation.

150	## 12. Decisions, each with the ways not taken
151	
152	- **The lock's shape.** Candidates:
153	  - `synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name))` around the whole of `loadClass`, which is the loader's own monitor. Taken.
154	  - The same with `registerAsParallelCapable`, one lock per name.
155	  - A lock only in `loadClosureClass`.
156	  - A `ConcurrentHashMap` of futures per name.
157	
158	  The monitor is the lock the JVM already holds when it resolves a class through a loader that is not parallel-capable, and it is what the JDK's own `loadClass` takes. Explicit loads (`loadClosureClass`, `getRTTIclass`, the union instantiation) were the only ones running without it. Taking it adds no lock order the implicit loads do not already have: a generation step that initialises another class under the monitor, as `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:274` can, already does so on every implicit load. Per-name locks would admit two loads each holding one name's lock while generating a class that needs the other's; the JDK leaves them off unless a loader opts in. A lock in `loadClosureClass` alone leaves the other two explicit callers racing. Futures would change the loader's structure for no gain the measurement can see.
159	- **Where `history` is written.** Left before `defineClass`. Under the lock no other thread can see the name before its class is defined. Moving the write would change what the same thread does if generation re-enters the loader for the name it is generating, which it does not today by reading, and every single-thread run would need re-measuring for no gain. The pre-existing behaviour after a failed load, where the name stays in `history` and a later load of it returns null (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:189-193`), is unchanged; by reading, not measured.
160	- **Binding a catch name always.** The grammar makes the name mandatory (`try.tex:22`), and the specification binds it (`:56-60`), so every catch clause's code changes: `getValue`, a cast and a store in place of a pop. The prelude has no `catch`, so no library class moves. The other way, binding only a name the body reads, needs a free-variable test at each clause and saves three instructions.

%lhs = rhs
%- aSeparateExpression
%
%postProfit(revenue
%           - expenses)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{lhs} = \VAR{rhs}\)\\
\(- \VAR{aSeparateExpression}\)\\[4pt]
\(\VAR{postProfit}(\null\)\pushtabs\=\+\(\VAR{revenue}\)\\
\(           - \VAR{expenses})\)\-\\\poptabs
\end{Fortress}

\item[pasted]
Fortress has special syntax for matrix pasting.  Within square
brackets, whitespace-separated expressions are treated (depending
on their type) as either matrix elements or submatrices within a
row.  Because whitespace is the separator, it also ends expressions
where possible.  In addition, newline-or-semicolon-separated
rows are pasted vertically along their columns.  Higher-dimensional
pasting is expressed with repeated semicolons, but repeated newlines
do not have the same effect.
%id2a = [ 1 0 ; 0 1 ]
%id2b = [ 1 0 ;
%         0 1 ]
%id2c = [ 1 0
%         0 1 ]
%cube2 = [ 1 0 ; 0 1 ;; 1 -1 ; 1 1 ]
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{id2a} = [1\;0 ; 0\;1\,]\)\\
\(\VAR{id2b} = [\null\)\pushtabs\=\+\(1\;0 ;\)\\
\(         0\;1\,]\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\VAR{id2c} = [\null\)\pushtabs\=\+\(1\;0\)\\
\(         0\;1\,]\)\-\\\poptabs
\({cube}_{2} = [1\;0 ; 0\;1 ;; 1 -1 ; 1\;1\,]\)
\end{Fortress}

followed by \KWD{of}, a sequence of typecase clauses
(each consisting of a sequence of \emph{guarding types}
followed by the token \EXP{\Rightarrow}, followed by an expression block),
an optional \KWD{else} clause
(consisting of \KWD{else} followed by the token \EXP{\Rightarrow},
followed by an expression block),
and finally \KWD{end}.

A \KWD{typecase} expression with a binding expression
evaluates the expression first;
if it completes normally, the value of the expression is bound
to the identifiers and the first matching typecase clause is chosen.
If there are multiple identifiers, the binding expression must be evaluated
to a tuple value of the same number of elements.
A typecase clause matches if the type of the value bound to each identifier
is a subtype of the corresponding type in the clause.
The expression block of the first matched clause
(and only that clause) is evaluated (see \secref{block-expr}) to yield
the value of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
If no matched clause is found, a \TYP{MatchFailure} exception is thrown
(\TYP{MatchFailure} is an unchecked exception).

### Counts by kind

Method: one bucket per row, from the **first-named class** in its class cell —

independent Run C3 (`run-c3/gaps.md`, rows 156-172, reproducers in

Made 2026-09-28 on `main` at `f052e82f5`, over the batch's five commits: `079f54ea9` (Y), `d8e0cd28e` (X), `d357c9cc4` (the first review's corrections), `18e4ffabe` (the judge's ruling) and `f052e82f5` (the repair). The script runs the gate again after this review (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:1896-1907`). - **Batch rule 1, from the hunks.**
  - Y's hunks: the comment above `isEligibleToExtend`, the disjunct and the new method (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:252-255`, `:261-262`, `:273-287`), and three new compiler tests.
  - X's hunks: `Specification/basic/traits.tex:235-267`, a new subsection inserted into `Specification/appendices/changes.tex` (94 lines, `:1246-1338`, no line removed), and the citation digits of two test messages.
  - The repair's hunks: one line, `changes.tex:1309`, and three new files, `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXComprisesMeetWalk.fss`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXComprisesMeetCompiled.fss` and its `.test`. Their component names are new, and their traits are local to each component.
  - No declaration, method, trait body or operator is changed twice.
- **Rule 2.** The repair's tests hold the Meet Rule's example, which has no parameterized trait. The base's checker and rung Y's refuse it alike (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-7C/merged-tests/between-y.txt`), so the tests depend on neither rung's edit. X's Effect depends on Y's code: that is the one dependence, and `landsOnlyWith` holds it.
- **The landed method against the approved shadow.** `TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:275-287` is `explorations/reviews/anyintegral-comprises-ways/shadow-thc.py:52-64` byte for byte (`diff`). The disjunct at `:260-263` is the shadow's `:45-49` with two things removed: the broad form's disjunct `(aicwRelax && !tt.getArgs.isEmpty) ||`, and `aicwNarrow &&`.
- **Footers.** The footers on all five commits are exact. No commit's message or added lines carry a model identifier. `079f54ea9`, `d8e0cd28e` and `f052e82f5` touch paths outside `explorations/`, and each carries a `historical:` line naming the 2012 tree's files it edits. The two specification commits also name `Specification/fortress.pdf`, which the revival first committed (`414b790e3`), as batch 7R's `17c6052bb` did.

  - It has 491 rows: the base's 485 and rows 487 to 492. Row 148 is still the one vacant number, no number is duplicated, and the base's rows keep their order.

  - The counts by kind still cover rows 1 to 310. `FACTS.md`'s anchors `:680` and `:820` hold.

  - The published `Specification/fortress.pdf` has 627 pages and prints the repaired Effect sentence (`pdftotext`). Its sha256 is the one `REPAIR-review.md` section 3 gives.

- **Tracked paths.** Every path the landed records cite resolves to a tracked file or directory, including the rung-relative `probes/` paths.     It's mostly subtypes of Range that are interesting.

    The partial order on ranges describes containment:
      a < b iff all points in a are strictly contained in b.
 **)
trait Range[\I\] extends { StandardPartialOrder[\Range[\I\]\], Contains[\I\] }
        excludes { Number, String } (* Important or the strided factories can't overload! *)
    getter stride(): I
    getter left(): Maybe[\I\]
    getter right(): Maybe[\I\]
    getter extent(): Maybe[\I\]
end

trait CompactFullRange[\I\] extends FullRange[\I\]
    getter lower(): I = self.left.get
    getter upper(): I = self.right.get
    opr |self| : ZZ32 = do
      (l, u) = (self.lower, self.upper)
      typecase l of
        l':ZZ32 => 0 MAX ((u - l') + 1)
        l':(ZZ32, ZZ32) => do (l1, l2) = l'; (u1, u2) = u; (0 MAX ((u1 - l1) + 1)) (0 MAX ((u2 - l2) + 1)) end
        l':(ZZ32, ZZ32, ZZ32) => do (l1, l2, l3) = l'; (u1, u2, u3) = u; (0 MAX ((u1 - l1) + 1)) (0 MAX ((u2 - l2) + 1))
      end
    end
    forward(): CompactFullRange[\I\] = self
end

component SkTryInArm
export Executable

object Oops(code: ZZ32) extends CheckedException end
boomU(k: ZZ32): () = throw Oops(k)
var hit: ZZ32 = 0
note(k: ZZ32): () = atomic do hit := hit + k end

tryInArm(k: ZZ32): () = do
  do
    note(1)
  also do
    try boomU(k) catch e Oops => note(e.code) end
  end
end

run(): () = do
  tryInArm(5)
  println("hit " hit.asString)
end

end
----
component SkTupleClauseSpread
export Executable

second(a: ZZ32, s: String): String = s || a.asString

localHead(z: ZZ32): String = do
  t: (ZZ32, String) = (z, "s")
  typecase t of
      p: (ZZ32, String) => second(p)
      else => "other"
    end
end

run(): () = do
  z: ZZ32 = 3 + 4
  println(localHead(z))
end

end

content.content:
\Method{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{GCD}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Z})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{LCM}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Z})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}

The operator \OPR{GCD} computes the greatest common divisor of its two arguments.
The result is always nonnegative.  If either argument is \EXP{0}, the result
is the absolute value of the other argument.

The operator \OPR{LCM} computes the least common multiple of its two arguments.
The result is always nonnegative.  If either argument is \EXP{1}, the result
is the absolute value of the other argument.  If either argument is \EXP{0}, the result is \EXP{0}.

The strictly positive integers form a partial order and lattice with
the ``evenly divides'' operator \EXP{\mid} as the partial order operator and
with \OPR{GCD} and \OPR{LCM} as the lattice operators.


%%   property FORALL (m, n) ((m GCD n) | m) AND ((m GCD n) | n)
%%   property FORALL (m, n) (m | (m LCM n)) AND (n | (m LCM n))
%%   property FORALL (m, n) (m GCD n) DOT (m LCM n) = |m DOT n|
\begin{Fortress}
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{property} \forall (m, n)\; ((m \OPR{GCD} n) \mid m) \wedge ((m \OPR{GCD} n) \mid n)\)\\
\(  \KWD{property} \forall (m, n)\; (m \mid (m \OPR{LCM} n)) \wedge (n \mid (m \OPR{LCM} n))\)\\
\(  \KWD{property} \forall (m, n)\; (m \OPR{GCD} n) \cdot (m \OPR{LCM} n) = \left|m \cdot n\right|\)\-\\\poptabs
\end{Fortress}
\revision{revival-gcd}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that the result
equals the other argument where the two paragraphs above now say its absolute
value, as the first sentence of each requires when the other argument is
negative, and its last property equated the product of the two results with
\EXP{m \cdot n}, which nonnegative results satisfy only up to sign.
On a fixed-size integer type, a result that the type cannot hold throws an
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} (\chapref{operators}).}

\section{Operators and Their Properties}
\seclabel{opr-properties}


For some types, such as the integers \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} or the rationals \EXP{\mathbb{Q}},
results are always exact, and algebraic properties can be expected to be obeyed exactly.
For other types, such as floating-point numbers, results are not always numerically
exact, and algebraic properties can be expected to be obeyed only approximately.
For example, given three floating-point values \VAR{a} and \VAR{b} and \VAR{c},
it may well be that \EXP{a+(b+c)} is not equal to \EXP{(a+b)+c}; but we would expect
their values to be reasonably close---unless, of course, overflow occurred in one
expression but not the other.

\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
\vskip-\lastskip
A \emph{semilattice} is a set of values with an operator \EXP{\sqcap} that is commutative, associative, and idempotent.
Examples of such operators are \EXP{\wedge}, \EXP{\vee}, \EXP{\cap}, \EXP{\cup}, \OPR{MAX}, \OPR{MIN}, \OPR{GCD}, and \OPR{LCM}.
